before: A separate four-node CC2538 pilot moves observation construction, frozen attention inference, hop HMAC, replay checks and signed-receipt processing into the compiled MCU image. The host triggers traffic and authenticated beacon exchange and records UART output; it does not choose ordinary next hops or seal ordinary data and receipts. Node-local cache, link estimates and service debts reconstruct the 93-element observation. The original three-hop chain and a geometry with two feasible source choices each offer ten packets. Table 10 separates these public-fixture runs from two longer, separately provisioned runs. These functional fixtures are not independent statistical replicates of the original benchmark.
after: The four-node CC2538 pilot executes observation construction, frozen attention inference, hop authentication and receipt handling inside the MCU. The host triggers traffic and beacon exchange and captures UART output. Earlier public fixtures deliver twenty packets and verified receipts, with fifty matching routing decisions. Table 10 compares the retained private-key FP32 streams with two later implementations; each profile offers one hundred packets in a three-hop chain and one hundred in a geometry with two feasible source choices. These are sequential functional diagnostics, not independent statistical replicates or a new confirmatory comparison; N is the offered count.

before: Every MCU decision matches the frozen Python actor, and an independent feature reconstruction differs by less than 1e-4. Captured ordinary hop tags, source authenticators and sink signatures are checked independently. Exact replay, a corrupt hop tag, a corrupt source tag inside a valid hop envelope, and a forged sink signature inside a valid hop envelope are rejected. The longer version additionally rejects an authenticated stale boot session and repeated provisioning. It receives fresh random pairwise keys and a sink signing seed over the trusted emulator-control UART; a locked, persisted host allocator reserves new 64-bit boot sessions before startup. Private audit fixtures remain outside the public repository. These are emulator provisioning controls, not protected MCU storage or persistent device firmware.
after: Operation-level profiling identifies approximately 270 ms per-hop FP32 inference and 81 ms Ed25519 verification in the declared emulator. A separate Q22 implementation uses signed 32-bit weights and activations, 64-bit accumulators and an 8193-point tanh lookup table. Export checks bound arithmetic for input coordinates in [−32, 32]; nonfinite or out-of-domain inputs are rejected. The lookup table adds 32,772 bytes beyond the 176,644 parameter bytes. All five hundred retained decisions and the later MCU decisions match the FP32 reference at their recorded observations, with logit errors below 1e-4. This is tested approximation agreement, not universal action equivalence. Inference falls to approximately 12–13 ms with one candidate. Caching the provisioned sink signing key also removes repeated key derivation from the packet path.

before: The first kernel evaluated masked candidates unnecessarily and allowed relay cache expiry; its failed development capture is retained. Skipping only masked computations restores the declared freshness behavior without changing weights or extending timing windows. The O2-compiled version uses a rolling source-identity replay window to support longer sequential streams; it does not establish deadline compliance. The original runs take 1119–1128 ms in the chain and 915–922 ms in the choice geometry; seven of ten receipts in each miss their 90 or 350 ms class budget. Table 10 reports the longer-run delays without treating delivery as real-time success. All times come from the Renode SysTick model, not a physical board measurement.
after: The experimental fast profile adds a distinct 66-byte application frame: the fourteen-byte packet identity, a sixteen-byte source–sink HMAC, the twenty-byte hop header and its sixteen-byte hop tag. The sink emits this private receipt after verifying source data, then generates the original Ed25519 proof. Relays check the hop envelope and pending route and forward the private receipt opaquely; they assign no forwarding credit from it. Only the source authenticates the end-to-end MAC and settles its service debt early. The separate public proof remains subject to Ed25519 verification and the original MAC-ACK credit gate. A private MAC is not transferable public evidence, and its deadline endpoint is not the original signed-receipt endpoint.

before: The pilot fixes source 0, sink 3 and four provisioned nodes, with sixteen pending records. Beacon energy and queue inputs are nominal, not measured telemetry; beacon scheduling is test-triggered. Longer streams test state reuse and replay-window progression rather than network-size scaling. Worst-case stack, overload, interference, autonomous rendezvous, real board startup, reboot-safe MCU storage and measured RF/energy remain outside this validation. The private-key version requires locally retained private fixtures for retrospective hop-tag audit; public-fixture captures remain fully inspectable. None of these runs supports a neural-superiority or deployment-readiness claim.
after: Fixed-point inference reduces signed-receipt misses from 134/200 to 68/200; the 90 ms class still fails. In the fast profile, all two hundred private receipts meet their source deadlines, while all two hundred deferred Ed25519 proofs are eventually verified and sixty-eight miss the original signed deadline. Extra private receipts add three radio frames per chain packet or two per choice packet; no energy saving is inferred. Tested-path stack watermarks reach 6624 bytes, with 3968 static RAM bytes and intact guards under the 32 KiB linker budget. These are observed paths, not a worst-case stack bound.

before: Missing forwarding evidence can reflect packet loss, contention or an unobserved transmission, making feedback design a joint problem of inference and airtime. We benchmark ACK-gated censored passive feedback against active proofs in 750 IEEE 802.15.4 runs on 30 new fixtures, with naive-passive, frozen-prior and capacity-matched policy controls. Under blackholes, delivery increases from 71.28% to 75.94%, a paired gain of 4.67 percentage points (95% interval 2.36–6.97; Holm-adjusted p=0.0161). Energy per delivered byte falls while total modeled radio energy rises slightly. The controls do not establish a unique censoring or attention advantage. A separate 180-run experiment tests frozen policies over authenticated messages and node-local records. Attention delivers 81.61% in benign conditions and 61.11% under selective dropping, without an established advantage over greedy or multilayer-perceptron routing. Serial-interface testing identifies and corrects a receive-time freshness error. Earlier UART-to-radio firmware runs on four emulated Cortex-M3 boards; neural inference and cryptography execute on the host PC. Each host-policy control delivers ten of ten packets. A further 240-run factorial study separates proof traffic from evidence handling; adding proofs reduces delivery by 6.11 percentage points with always-on listening. A four-node MCU emulation pilot executes live routing and authentication but misses the two tighter receipt deadlines. An exploratory 60–300 s extension exposes routing-energy exhaustion and increasing service debt. The contribution is a traceable comparison of feedback mechanisms and transport boundaries; the evidence does not establish sustained operation, physical-board performance, measured energy consumption or absolute deadline compliance.

before: ACK-gated censored passive feedback passed the prespecified replacement test on 30 new fixtures, improving blackhole delivery over active proofs by 4.67 percentage points. The matched controls establish neither a unique censoring effect nor an attention advantage. In the separate 180-run authenticated transport study, frozen policies operate on received wire state and local service records without an established attention benefit. Serial-interface testing corrected a receive-time error, and four emulated Cortex-M3 boards execute the compiled UART-to-radio bridge while inference and cryptography run on the host in that earlier fixture. The 60–300 s extension exposes routing-energy exhaustion and increasing source debt. Together, these results define the benchmark’s supported feedback comparison and deployment boundary: absolute service compliance, physical-board operation, physical on-board policy/crypto execution and measured energy remain unvalidated. The 240-run factorial extension identifies a proof-traffic delivery penalty with always-on listening, while severe loss under periodic sleeping limits transfer of that finding. Isolated Cortex-M3 execution verifies actor outputs and cryptographic primitives, not a complete embedded radio system. A four-node emulated live-path pilot now performs routing and authentication inside the MCU, including longer private-key runs. Successful delivery does not establish real-time service: receipt delays exceed the two tighter class budgets.
